prayer.text: Saint Anthony Mary Zaccaria, pray for us.

cues.text: A Physician's Compassion

Born at Cremona in 1502, Anthony lost his father as an infant and was raised by his young widowed mother, who instilled in him a deep compassion for the poor by making him her own almoner from childhood.
He studied medicine at Padua and earned his doctorate at twenty-two, returning to Cremona to practice among the city's poor.
From Physician to Priest
Even while practicing medicine, Anthony felt an increasing pull toward direct spiritual ministry, and began teaching catechism to children and the poor at the church of San Vitale in Cremona.
Formally renouncing any future family inheritance, he was ordained a priest in 1528, at his first Mass reportedly experiencing a vision of angels present at the altar.
A Response to a Corrupted Milan
Sent to Milan, Anthony encountered widespread moral decay that troubled him deeply, and after prayerful discernment concluded that ordinary preaching alone was insufficient to the crisis.
Together with Bartolomeo Ferrari and Giacomo Antonio Morigia, he founded a new community in 1530, the Clerics Regular of St. Paul .
It later became commonly known as the Barnabites , after the Milanese church of St. Barnabas that became their headquarters.
Eucharistic Reforms
Anthony introduced a number of devotional innovations that were genuinely bold for his era.
He encouraged frequent, even daily, reception of Communion at a time when this was uncommon practice.

He promoted the Forty Hours' Devotion of continuous Eucharistic adoration and instituted the custom, still observed in some places, of ringing church bells at three o'clock every Friday afternoon in memory of Christ's death on the Cross.
Founding a Wider Reform Movement
Beyond the Barnabites, Anthony co-founded with Countess Ludovica Torelli a corresponding congregation of religious women, the Angelic Sisters of St. Paul.

He also established a lay association allowing married and single laypeople to participate directly in apostolic renewal—an unusually inclusive vision of Church reform for his era, later echoed in the twentieth century's own emphasis on the lay apostolate.
Legacy
Twice denounced to Rome on suspicion of heresy for his innovations, Anthony was fully exonerated both times.
Worn out at only thirty-six by his relentless labors, he fell ill while on a peacemaking mission and died at his mother's home in Cremona in 1539.

Canonized in 1897 by Pope Leo XIII, he is remembered as a physician of both bodies and souls whose reforming zeal anticipated currents of renewal the wider Church would not fully embrace for centuries.
